title: Promising not to change
objectives: Use `const` on variables, references and methods.
Predict which lines a `const` promise makes the compiler reject.

screens.title: A tick size that cannot move
screens.prose: A tick is the smallest price step an exchange allows. In Python a name can always be pointed at a new value. In C++ you can forbid it with `const`.
screens.question: What happens when you build `main.cpp`?

options.why: That is the Python habit of rebinding a name. `const` forbids any assignment after the declaration.

options.text: It builds, and line 3 is ignored, so `tick` stays 0.01
options.why: C++ never ignores a line silently. Breaking a `const` promise is a compile error.

options.text: It builds, then stops with an error when line 3 runs
options.why: `const` is checked by the compiler, before the program ever runs.

hints.text: When is `const` checked: while compiling, or while running?
Line 3 assigns to `tick`, which line 2 declared `const`.
The compiler checks every assignment against the type. `const double` cannot be assigned, so the build fails at line 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. `const` is a promise the compiler checks before anything runs.

byKey.five: That is the Python habit of rebinding a name. `const` forbids any assignment after the declaration.

explain.text: The compiler checks every assignment against the variable's type. `tick` is a `const double`, so line 3 is a compile error, and clang names both lines. No program is built.

Only `px` carries `const`. `out` is a new local copy.
Line 4 writes through `px`, which is read only. Lines 3 and 5 change `out` and `fee`, which are ordinary copies.

screens.title: What a promise buys
screens.prose: A `const` reference parameter is a **const reference**: the function may read the caller's object but never change it. Here is the version *without* `const`, and three calls.
screens.question: With this plain `std::vector<double>&`, which calls compile?

options.why: A plain reference may change its object. So the compiler refuses a temporary, which has no variable, and `fixed`, which is `const`.
`fixed` is `const`. Binding a plain reference to it would let `mean` change it, so clang says it "would lose const qualifier".
`{101.5, 99.0}` is a temporary. A plain reference must name a real variable, so clang says it "expects an lvalue".

hints.text: A plain reference says the function might change the argument. Which arguments must not be changed, or cannot be?
`fixed` is `const`, and `{101.5, 99.0}` is a temporary with no name.
Only `prices` is a non-const variable. Adding `const` to the parameter makes all three calls compile.

feedback.correct: Only a non-const variable binds to a plain reference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which arguments the function would be allowed to change.

byKey.all: A plain reference may change its object, so it refuses the temporary and the `const` vector.

explain.text: A plain reference may change its argument, so it accepts only a non-const variable. With `const std::vector<double>& v`, all three calls compile. That is why read-only parameters are `const&`: they take anything.

screens.title: Const objects, const methods
screens.prose: `const` after a method's parameter list promises the method does not change the object. A `const` object may only call such methods.

screens.title: Write spread
screens.prose: The data in `Quote` is private: read it through the `const` getters `bid()` and `ask()`. The starter breaks two rules.

`bid_` and `ask_` are private. The getters are `bid()` and `ask()`, with brackets.
Write `double spread(const Quote& q) { return q.ask() - q.bid(); }`. The getters are `const`, so a `const Quote&` may call them.

screens.title: Known before the program runs
screens.prose: `constexpr` asks for more than `const`: the value must be known while compiling. The compiler can then fold it into the code. `read_tick` reads a config file when the program starts.

`read_tick()` runs only when the program starts.
Line 5 asks for a compile-time value from a run-time call. Line 6 is fine: `const` only forbids changes later.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the `constexpr` whose value needs the program to run.

screens.title: Const is a view, not a freeze

state.caption: Two names, one vector; the dashed name is read only

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You treated `const` as freezing the vector. It only stops changes made through `view`; `px` may still change it, and `view` sees the change.
`px` is not `const`, so `px[0] = 99.0` is allowed. Only writes through `view` are refused.

hints.text: How many vectors are there?
`view` and `px` name the same box.
`px[0] = 99.0` changes the one vector. `view[0]` reads that vector, so it prints 99.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the vectors, then ask which name did the writing.

byKey.hundred: You treated `const` as freezing the vector. It only stops changes made through `view`; `px` changed it.

explain.text: There is one vector with two names. `const` restricts the name `view`, so `view[0] = 1` would not compile, but `px` is free to write. `view[0]` then reads the changed value, 99.

A local `std::vector<double> out = px;` is your own copy.
Copy into `out`, add `fee` to each `out[i]`, and `return out;`. Returning it is free: copy elision.

screens.title: Four places for const
screens.prose:
Every `const` you used is a promise the compiler checks.

```cpp
const double tick = 0.01;     // never reassigned
constexpr int lot = 100;      // known while compiling
double spread(const Quote& q);// reads q, no copy
double mid() const;           // does not change *this
```
screens.question: A `const Quote q` can call which of its methods?

options.why: A method without `const` may change the object, so the compiler stops a `const` object calling it.

options.text: None of them: it can only read members
options.why: Methods marked `const` are allowed, and getters such as `bid()` are written that way.

feedback.correct: Only methods that promise not to change it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think back to `widen` and `mid`.

explain.text: A `const` object can read its members and call `const` methods. Mark every method that does not change the object `const`, or `const` callers cannot use it.

screens.title: Read it right to left
screens.prose: The next lesson builds pointers: `double* p` holds the address of a `double`, and `*p` is the `double` there. A declaration reads from the name outwards, right to left. Here is `const double* const p`.
screens.question: Put the reading of `const double* const p` in order.

lines.text: a `const`: the `const` next to `p` fixes `p` itself
pointer to: the `*` to its left
a `const double`: the type it points at is read only

hints.text: Start at the name and move left one piece at a time.
Directly left of `p` is `const`; left of that is `*`.
`p` is a `const` pointer to a `const double`: neither `p` nor `*p` can change.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin at `p` and walk left.

byKey.cd: The type pointed at is the last thing you reach, at the far left.

explain.text: From the name: `p` is `const`, then `*` makes it a pointer, then `const double` is what it points at. So `p` cannot be pointed elsewhere and `*p` cannot be changed. `double const` and `const double` read the same.

screens.title: Two kinds of const pointer
screens.prose: Use the right-to-left reading. A `const` next to the name fixes the pointer; a `const` next to `double` fixes the value it points at.
screens.question: Fill in Yes or No for each declaration.

hints.text: Read each declaration from `p` leftwards.
`const double* p`: `p` is a pointer to a `const double`. The pointer itself is not `const`.
Row 2: No, Yes. Row 3: `p` is a `const` pointer to `double`: Yes, No. Row 4: No, No.

feedback.correct: `const` binds to what sits on its left, or to its right when nothing is on its left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each line right to left from `p`.

explain.text: `const double* p` is a pointer to read-only values: `*p = 3` fails, `p = &y` is fine. `double* const p` is the reverse: clang says "cannot assign to variable 'p' with const-qualified type 'double *const'". With both, neither can change.

screens.title: A market-data callback
screens.question: Why does the callback take `const Tick&`?

options.text: No copy per call, and no strategy can change the tick the next one sees
`const` makes the compiler run strategies in parallel
options.why: `const` says nothing about threads. It forbids writes through `t` and avoids a copy.

options.text: `const&` keeps the tick alive after the callback returns
options.why: The feed owns the tick and may reuse it after the call. A strategy that needs it later must copy it.

options.text: A plain `Tick&` would copy the tick
options.why: A plain reference copies nothing either. It would let a strategy change the tick for every other strategy.

hints.text: Two costs matter here: copying, and one strategy breaking another.
Each tick goes to many strategies in turn.
`&` avoids copying the string and three numbers. `const` stops one strategy editing the tick the next one reads.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about copies, and about the strategies that read the same tick later.

byKey.plainref: A plain reference avoids the copy too, but any strategy could change the tick for the others.

explain.text: `&` means the handler passes its own tick without copying the symbol string. `const` means no strategy can edit it before the next one reads it. A strategy that keeps ticks must copy them, because the feed reuses its buffer.

ideas: `const` is a promise the compiler checks. A `const` variable is never reassigned, and a `const&` parameter is only read.
A `const` reference accepts variables, `const` objects and temporaries; a `const` object can call only methods marked `const`.
`const` restricts one name, not the object: another name may still change it. `constexpr` also demands the value while compiling.

formula.name: Reading a declaration
formula.tex: \texttt{const double* const p} \quad\to\quad p \text{ is a const pointer to a const double}
formula.note: Start at the name and read leftwards; `const int` and `int const` are the same.

summary.trap: A `const&` view is not a frozen copy: if the object changes through another name, the view sees the change.

options.text: Both `const int lots = 5;` and `int const lots = 5;`

options.why: `const` may sit either side of `int`; both lines declare the same type.
`const int` and `int const` are the same type, so both are read only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does the side of `int` that `const` sits on change the type?

explain.text: For a plain type, `const int` and `int const` mean the same. The position matters only around a `*`, where it decides whether the pointer or the value is fixed.

quiz.question: A desk reads its risk limits from `desk.ini` once, at start-up, and never changes them. Which declaration fits?

options.why: `constexpr` needs the value while compiling, but the file is read only when the program runs.
That works, but nothing stops a later line changing the limits by mistake.

feedback.correct: Set once at start-up, then read only.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. When is the value known, and should it ever change?

explain.text: The limits are known only when the program runs, so `constexpr` is impossible. `const` fixes them after that one load, and the compiler rejects any later write.

options.text: Yes: a `const` reference can bind to a temporary
No: a reference needs a named variable
